A warming young sun hangs low and gold on the horizon, its light spilling across the new green and the old red rock alike.
A large pale moon hangs in a sky that is just beginning to blue, orbital mirrors glinting like new stars beside it.
A great partner-planet hangs huge in the sky beyond the terraformed valley, banded and serene above the spreading green.
The curve of the planet sweeps below, the terminator line dividing rust desert from the creeping green of new life.
Orbital mirrors catch the sun and scatter bright points across a dust-pink sky slowly deepening toward true blue.
A comet trails its silver veil across the upper atmosphere, seeding ice into the warming world below.
The old red desert stretches flat to one horizon while new green pushes toward it from the other, meeting in a blurred frontier.
A ringed giant hangs tilted in the afternoon sky, its rings catching light above the first shallow rivers.
A distant mountain range catches the last red light, its peaks dusted with the first thin frost of a changing climate.
The sky shifts in gradients from deep dust-pink at the horizon to a fragile, promising blue directly overhead.
Two moons rise together over the ridge, one large and cratered, one small and fast, above a green that barely exists yet.
A loose constellation of orbital mirrors drifts in slow formation, each one a bright comma written across the twilight.
The sun sets behind a low ridge and the sky burns amber and rose, the air just thick enough to scatter color.
A vast impact crater fills the middle distance, its floor pooled with the first standing water this world has ever held.
From high above, the patchwork of red and green and silver water makes the planet look like something being assembled by hand.
A thin aurora ripples green and violet near the poles as the young magnetosphere stirs and strengthens.
The partner-planet rises full and banded at dusk, casting faint colored shadows across the new grass below.
A chain of orbital habitats catches the morning sun, strung like beads across the pale arc of low orbit.
Dust storms swirl red at the desert edge while clear sky opens wide and blue over the greened lowlands beyond.
The horizon glows with the long polar summer, the sun barely dipping before it rises again over the ice retreat.
A meteor shower streaks silently overhead, dozens of bright lines dissolving in an atmosphere just dense enough to burn them.
The young sun climbs through thin cloud, its light still cool and golden, not yet the white of a mature day.
A dry river valley is wet at last, the first trickle catching sunlight between banks of rust and new moss.
High cirrus clouds streak a sky caught between pink and blue, the first water-ice clouds this atmosphere has ever made.
The full disk of the partner-planet reflects enough light to cast soft shadows at midnight over the terraformed plain below.
